text: Thérèse Schwartze got her first training from her father, the painter Johan Georg Schwartze. She studied for a year at the Rijksacademie and then went to Munich to work under Gabriel Max and Franz von Lenbach. In 1879 she went to Paris to study with Jean-Jacques Henner. Back in Amsterdam she joined Arti et Amicitiae, and she showed her work at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago. Most of her sitters came from the city's elite. She married Anton van Duyl late in life and then added his name to her signature.

Eduard Veith first trained to follow his father, a decorative painter. He went on to Vienna to study at the Museum of Applied Arts under Ferdinand Laufberger, and he made sgraffito for exhibition buildings at the Paris Exposition Universelle. Back home he helped his father paint churches and synagogues. After study trips to Italy, Belgium and Tunisia he settled in Vienna as a freelance artist. Franz Joseph I ordered the big ceiling fresco he painted in the Maria-Theresia-Saal of the Hofburg. He died in Vienna in 1925.

Adolphe Willette studied for four years at the École des Beaux-Arts under Alexandre Cabanel. He made Pierrot an imaginary hero of France. His work ranged from dainty trifles to political satire, and the guillotine and Death appear in his caricatures. He sent many drawings to the French illustrated press, some under pen names such as Cémoi and Pierrot. He also painted walls, stained glass and a ceiling for cabarets and music halls, among them Le Chat noir and La Cigale. During the Dreyfus affair he sided against Dreyfus and moved to the political right with Jean-Louis Forain.

Jan Davidsz. de Heem studied first under his father, a painter, and then under Balthasar van der Ast. He spent a few years in Leiden, where he also took lessons from David Bailly. After that he moved to the Southern Netherlands and joined the Guild of Saint Luke in Antwerp in 1635 or 1636. He was so much in demand that he could hardly meet the orders. A portrait of Prince William III in a frame of flowers and fruit sold for two thousand guilders. He died in Antwerp before the end of April 1684.

Elin Danielson's father went bankrupt when the family farm failed in the Finnish famine, and her mother took on many jobs to pay for her daughters' schooling. At 15 she moved to Helsinki to study at the Academy of Fine Arts. Later she took lessons at the Académie Colarossi in Paris. A scholarship took her to Florence, and a year later she moved to the village of Antignano, where she met the painter Raffaello Gambogi, who was 13 years younger. They began working together. They married in 1898, and she died in Antignano in 1919, mostly forgotten in Finland.

By the age of 15 El Lissitzky was already teaching students of his own. The St. Petersburg Academy of Arts turned him down, so he went to Germany in 1909 to study architectural engineering at the Darmstadt Polytechnic Institute. He worked as a bricklayer on the side. He began his career illustrating Yiddish children's books, and later he worked with Kazimir Malevich on suprematism and developed his own Proun series. In 1921 he moved to the Weimar Republic. He brought big changes to typography, exhibition design and book design.

Simeon Solomon got his first painting lessons from his older brother Abraham around 1850. As a student at the Royal Academy Schools he met Dante Gabriel Rossetti, the poet Swinburne and Edward Burne-Jones. His first show at the Academy came in 1858. He painted scenes from the Hebrew Bible and genre pictures of Jewish life and rituals, along with the literary subjects the Pre-Raphaelites liked. A public scandal after his arrest in 1873 cut his career short. Oscar Wilde and Walter Pater collected his work.

Joris Hoefnagel's father dealt in diamonds and luxury goods, and the family expected the son to join the business. He got a broad humanistic education. He called himself self-taught as an artist, but Karel van Mander wrote that Hans Bol gave him his first lessons. In his youth he spent time in France and Spain, and Seville fascinated him. After Spanish troops sacked Antwerp in 1576 and much of the family fortune was lost, he left the city and traveled with his friend, the cartographer Abraham Ortelius, to Venice and Rome.

Erik Werenskiold grew up in Kongsvinger Fortress as the fourth son of its commander. On the advice of the painter Adolph Tidemand he went to a college for painters, and later he spent four years in Munich. A French art show there in 1879 changed his mind, because the work of Charles-François Daubigny convinced him that plein air painting beat German studio painting. In 1880 his right arm was paralyzed. After half a year of recovery he regained his health. He is especially known for his drawings for the folk tale collection of Asbjørnsen and Moe.

Albert Hahn's father painted signs and glass and made frames, and the family lived in what Hahn later called respectable poverty. At nine he developed tuberculosis in his vertebrae and could not finish school, and at twelve he was apprenticed to his father. Later he spent two years in a hospital. In 1896 he saw works by Van Gogh at an exhibition in Groningen, and they left a deep mark on his style. His growing interest in socialism led him to join the Social Democratic Workers' Party. His drawings of the railroad strikes of 1903 appear in history textbooks.

James Crowe Richmond worked for three years on the staff of Isambard Kingdom Brunel on the Great Western Railway. In 1850 he sailed to New Zealand with his younger brother Henry, and the two walked south from Auckland to Taranaki. He was elected to Parliament in 1860. Politics left him little spare time, but he kept painting and sketching, and he formed a lifelong friendship with John Gully. He is notable for his watercolours, though he won a silver medal for an oil painting at the Dunedin Exhibition in 1865.

Thomas Hearne lost his father at five. He moved with his mother to Brinkworth in Wiltshire, and as a teenager he was apprenticed to an uncle who was a pastry cook in Covent Garden. In 1763 the Royal Society of Arts gave him a prize of a guinea for a still life. By 1765 he was apprenticed to the engraver William Woollett. He spent three and a half years in the Leeward Islands after the governor commissioned 20 large landscapes. Later he drew the historic monuments of Britain, and William Byrne engraved the drawings.

Christian Rohlfs took up painting as a teenager while he recovered from an infection, and that infection later led to the amputation of a leg. In 1901 he moved to Hagen, where the collector Karl Ernst Osthaus gave him a studio in an estate that became the Museum Folkwang. Meetings with Edvard Munch and Emil Nolde, and the sight of works by Van Gogh, pushed him toward expressionism. He made his first prints at 60, after seeing a show by the group Die Brücke. The Nazis condemned his work as degenerate and removed it from public collections.

Franz Eybl was already at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna at the age of ten. He later studied history painting under Johann Peter Krafft, and much of his work shows it. After 1840 Ferdinand Georg Waldmüller influenced his use of light. He painted landscapes, genre scenes and history pictures, and he counted himself among the most important portrait painters in 19th century Austria, alongside Friedrich von Amerling. Eybl made over 400 lithographic portraits. A way in Leopoldau, Vienna, was named after him in 1933.

Jean Daullé's father was a silversmith, and at 14 the boy began training with an engraver named Robart at a priory in Abbeville. He then went to Paris. In 1735 Pierre-Jean Mariette noticed his work and gave him recommendations. Soon after, the painter Hyacinthe Rigaud wanted him as his official engraver. In 1742 he was received at the Académie Royale with a plate showing Rigaud painting his wife. He became Engraver to the King and trained Pierre-François Basan and Johann Wille.

Bernardo Strozzi became a friar at 17. He joined a Capuchin monastery and was known by the nickname il Cappuccino, and before that he had trained with Cesare Corte and then with Pietro Sorri, who steered him toward a more natural style. He left the monastery to care for his mother and unmarried sister, and he supported them with his paintings. Genoa's powerful Doria and Centurione families became his patrons. His order grew unhappy with the portraits and genre paintings he made. The conflict came to a head in 1630, when he refused to go back to the monastery.

Bernardino Luini came from Runo, a village near Lake Maggiore, and he moved to Milan with his father in 1500. Details of his life are scant. Some writers say he trained under Giovan Stefano Scotto, and others say he was a pupil of Ambrogio Bergognone. He belonged to the circle of Leonardo, and many of his works were once attributed to Leonardo himself. His first frescoes include an Adoration of the Magi in San Pietro in Luino. He was known especially for graceful female figures with elongated eyes, which Vladimir Nabokov called Luinesque.

Étienne Baudet came from Vineuil, in the county of Blois. He studied under Sébastien Bourdon and Cornelis Bloemaert and then went to Rome. In his earliest plates he followed the manner of Bloemaert and used the graver alone. After he returned to Paris he changed his manner and added the point, and his best prints, which look a lot like those of Jean Baptiste Poilly, came from this time. He chose his subjects from the work of masters from Italy and France. He became a member of the Royal Academy of Paris and died there in 1711.

Charles Léandre met the painter Émile Bin at 16, and Bin became his teacher. He also studied under Alexandre Cabanel, and in his twenties he won several awards. From 1887 he showed portraits and genre pictures at the Salon, but his popular fame came from his comic drawings and caricatures. He contributed to Le Rire and Le Figaro and published albums such as Nocturnes and Le Musée des souverains. He also made lithographs and many posters. In 1904 he created the Société des Peintres Humoristes.

Herbert Crowley drew The Wigglemuch, a symbolic comic strip that ran for 13 installments in the New York Herald in 1910. He was born in London, studied singing in Paris and became a trained musician, but his drawings led him to New York. He lived there for around 15 years. His paintings and sketches were shown in group and solo exhibitions, including the Armory Show in 1913. A year later he exhibited with Léon Bakst, and a catalog compared his work to that of William Blake. The Wigglemuch was the only comic strip collection he ever published.

Pier Francesco Mola moved to Rome at the age of four with his father, the painter Giovanni Battista Mola. He lived in Venice and Bologna for a time. Rome stayed his home for the rest of his life. He painted the fresco Joseph Making Himself Known to His Brethren in the gallery of Alexander VII in the Quirinal Palace in 1657. He is thought to have been better at small pictures, especially landscapes. His looser style and more natural colours set him apart from the strict classicism of Andrea Sacchi.

Oskar Schlemmer lost both parents around 1900, and he learned early to look after himself. As a teenager he worked as an apprentice in an inlay workshop and then in marquetry. He studied at the School of Applied Arts in Stuttgart and then at the state academy, under the landscape painters Christian Landenberger and Friedrich von Keller. In 1923 he became Master of Form at the Bauhaus theatre workshop. He is best known for Triadic Ballet, in which costumed actors turned into geometric forms of the human body. He called it a party of form and colour.

Gérard Audran got his first lessons in drawing and engraving from his father in Lyon, and then he followed his brother to Paris. In 1666 he engraved three scenes for Charles Le Brun, and the painter was pleased. He spent three years in Rome. Colbert admired his work so much that he persuaded Louis XIV to call him back to Paris, and there Audran became engraver to the king. His prints of Le Brun's Battles of Alexander are regarded as the best of his many works. In 1683 he published a book on the proportions of the human body.

Jean Baptiste Vanmour came from Valenciennes, a Flemish town that later became French. He studied in the studio of Jacques-Albert Gérin, and the Marquis de Ferriol noticed his work. Ferriol became French ambassador to Constantinople in 1699, and Vanmour went with him. There he was asked for one hundred oil paintings of the local people. A set of one hundred engravings after these portraits came out in 1714, and the book had a big influence in Western Europe and was published in at least five languages. Painting audiences with the Sultan became his specialty.

Pehr Hilleström grew up on the island of Väddö, where his uncle was the vicar. He was the eldest of twelve children. After training with Johan Philip Korn and at the Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts, he made a study trip to Paris, Belgium and Holland and became a master weaver. He painted about thirty portraits, and he made many genre paintings of people at their daily tasks in upper and middle class homes in Stockholm. Dresses and furniture were painted exactly as they looked. In 1810 he became director of the Royal Swedish Academy of Arts.

Domenico Gargiulo got the nickname Micco Spadaro because his father made swords. He trained in the workshop of the battle painter Aniello Falcone, along with Andrea di Leone and Salvator Rosa. His earliest known works are two dated circular genre scenes, the Fortune Teller and the Inn, both from 1636. Two years later he began the fresco decoration of the choir of the Frati Conversi in the Certosa di San Martino in Naples. The Carthusians then asked him to fresco the prior's apartment there with the Baptism, a View of Naples and landscapes with hermits.

Henryk Siemiradzki first learned painting from a schoolteacher in Kharkiv, a former student of Karl Briullov. He studied natural sciences at the university there, but he kept painting. After he gave up his scientific career he moved to Saint Petersburg and studied at the Imperial Academy of Arts, where he graduated with a gold medal. He then studied under Karl von Piloty in Munich. In 1872 he moved to Rome, built a studio there on Via Gaeta, and spent summers on his estate near Częstochowa. In 1879 he offered the huge Nero's Torches to the new Polish National Museum.

Bernard van Orley never went to Italy, but Italian Renaissance painting influenced him, especially Raphael. He was born and died in Brussels. The town council there used him as a sort of commissioner of the arts, and he was also court artist to the Habsburg rulers. He concentrated on designing his works and left much of the painting to others, and he left the weaving of his woven wall hangings and the making of his stained glass entirely to workshops. Because of this, his many surviving works vary a lot in quality.

Egbert van Drielst began to study painting in a factory in his native Groningen that mostly made lacquered objects. He soon went to Haarlem as an apprentice in the wallpaper factory of Jan Augustini. Later he worked in the wallpaper studio in Amsterdam, where he became friends with Adriaan de Lelie. He studied old masters such as Jacob van Ruisdael and Meindert Hobbema and tried to use their techniques in his nature studies. In 1768 he joined the Guild of Saint Luke in Amsterdam. He often drew the landscape of Drenthe, and people sometimes call him the Drentse Hobbema.

Richard Cosway went to London at twelve to take painting lessons. He studied briefly with Thomas Hudson and then with William Shipley, and by 1760 he ran his own business. He was elected an associate of the Royal Academy in its first group, and a full member the next March on the casting vote of Sir Joshua Reynolds. In Johan Zoffany's group portrait of academy members he appears on an extra strip of canvas at the right. His wife was the painter Maria Cosway, a close friend of Thomas Jefferson.

Rudolf Ernst began studies at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna at fifteen, encouraged by his father, the architect Leopold Ernst. In 1876 he settled in Paris, where he exhibited under the name Rodolphe Ernst. Trips to Spain, Morocco, Egypt and Istanbul gave him things to study and document. From 1885 he painted only orientalist subjects, especially mosque interiors and harem scenes, based on photographs and prints as well as his own memories. Later he set up a shop in Fontenay-aux-Roses that made faience tiles with orientalist themes. He lived a reclusive life.

Moïse Kisling studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Kraków with Józef Pankiewicz and left for Paris in 1910 at the age of 19. After moving to Montmartre he joined the School of Paris and grew close to Amedeo Modigliani and Jules Pascin. He painted many nudes and portraits. He became a French national in 1924, after he was wounded serving with the French Foreign Legion in World War I. In 1940 he rejoined the army, but he later moved to the United States because Jews in occupied France were under threat. After the war he returned to France.

Tobias Stimmer painted on the Strasbourg astronomical clock. He came from Schaffhausen and worked there, in Strasbourg and in Baden-Baden as a wall and portrait painter. He made a great number of drawings for woodcuts, such as Bible scenes and allegories, and the printer Sigmund Feyerabend in Frankfurt published them, as did Bernhart Jobin in Strasbourg. Stimmer followed Hans Holbein the Younger but developed his own mannerism. Wall paintings of his remain on the House zum Ritter in Schaffhausen, although that building was much restored.

Fernand Cormon's father was the playwright Eugène Cormon, and his mother, Charlotte Furais, was an actress. He studied under Alexandre Cabanel, Eugène Fromentin and Jean-François Portaels. His brush dwelled on scenes of bloodshed such as the Death of Ravana. He also painted large works with Stone Age themes for the Museum of natural history in Paris. He ran an art school, the Atelier Cormon, where he tried to guide his students toward pictures the Salon jury would accept. Toulouse-Lautrec and Louis Anquetin were among those he could not convince.

Jean Émile Laboureur came from a prosperous bourgeois family in Nantes. His father wanted him to study law, so he went to Paris in 1895, but he soon left to study fine arts at the Académie Julian, where Auguste-Louis Lepère taught him engraving. His first works were wood engravings on Primitivist themes. He began to call himself Jean Émile in the United States, which he first visited in 1904. After he settled in Paris he switched from wood engraving to etching. Even though he was conscripted in 1914, he published three series of engravings on war.

Willy Finch grew up in Ostend as the son of British parents. At 24 he studied for a year at the Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts in Brussels. In 1883 he became a founding member of Les XX, a group of twenty Belgian painters, designers and sculptors who rebelled against outmoded academism. Seurat and Signac impressed him, and he changed to a pointillist style. In the early 1890s he switched to pottery, because he could not make a living by painting. In 1897 Count Louis Sparre invited him to Porvoo in Finland to head the Iris ceramics factory.

Isaac van Ostade began his studies under his brother Adriaen and stayed with him until he started his own practice in 1641. Rembrandt influenced him early, and it shows in a Slaughtered Pig. For a time he painted peasant scenes like his brother's, but he got low prices and could only stay second to Adriaen. He gradually turned to landscapes in the manner of Esaias van de Velde, with village streets and frozen canals. His last series shows roadside inns with halts of travellers. He died in Haarlem in 1649 after painting about 400 pictures.

Adam Frans van der Meulen's father was a notary in Brussels, and Adam was the eldest of seven children. In 1651 he was registered at the Guild of Saint Luke as a pupil of Peter Snayers and became a master the same day. Snayers painted battles and hunting scenes. Van der Meulen went into the service of Louis XIV and painted the king's victories, new possessions and portraits. He helped shape the image of the king as the Sun King. His battle scenes influenced military painting in France.

Ernst Fries belonged, with Karl Philipp Fohr and Carl Rottmann, to the so-called triumvirate of Heidelberg Romanticism, and he was the youngest of the three. He was one of fifteen children of a banker, dye maker and art collector. His family's wealth let him travel freely and get a thorough artistic education. From 1810 he took lessons with Fohr and Rottmann from an engraver known as the University Sign Master. After that he studied with the landscape painter Carl Kuntz in Karlsruhe. In 1818 he went to Darmstadt for private lessons in perspective and architectural drawing.

Andrea del Sarto took his name from his father's trade, because his father Agnolo was a tailor. By 1494 he was apprenticed to a goldsmith, and then to a woodcarver and painter named Gian Barile, with whom he stayed until 1498. Vasari says he then went to Piero di Cosimo and later to Raffaellino del Garbo. With an older friend, Franciabigio, he opened a joint studio in the Piazza del Grano. People in his lifetime regarded him as an artist without errors. After his death Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael eclipsed his renown.

Gaspard Dughet never visited France, although people generally call him a French painter. He was born in Rome to a French pastry cook and his Italian wife. Between about 1631 and 1635 he was a pupil of Nicolas Poussin, who had married his sister Anne, so people widely knew him as Gaspard Poussin. After he left Poussin's studio his style became more fluid, and he painted storms, which make up 30 of his 400 known works. He specialised in landscapes of the Roman Campagna. Guillaume Courtois often painted the figures in his landscapes.

John Raphael Smith got his middle name from the artist Raphael, and his father was the painter Thomas Smith. After a short education at Derby School he was apprenticed to a linen-draper in the city, and his older brother Thomas Corregio Smith was a painter too. In 1767 he moved to London to start a print-making business, and he earned extra money from miniatures. Then he turned to engraving, and a mezzotint after Henry Benbridge launched his career. His Public Ledger plate was popular. He later reproduced some forty works of Sir Joshua Reynolds.

Cornelis Kruseman went to the Amsterdam drawing academy from the age of fourteen and had lessons from Charles Howard Hodges, Jean Augustin Daiwaille and Petrus Antonius Ravelli. He painted portraits and biblical scenes and also showed Italian peasant life. In 1821 he went to Paris and Italy, and he stayed in Italy for four years, working with and learning from Jean-Victor Schnetz and Louis Léopold Robert. He later published an account of the journey. In 1841 he went back to Italy for several years. People therefore also call him the Italian Kruseman.

Étienne Picart took the nickname le Romain after his stay in Rome, to tell himself apart from all the other engravers named Picart. He spent six years there, from 1655 to 1661, with his friend and fellow engraver Guillaume Vallet. He was the son of a Paris bookseller and learned his craft as an apprentice of Poilly the Elder. Back in Paris, the Royal Academy received both friends. He engraved works by Correggio and Poussin. In 1711 he left Paris to join his son, the engraver Bernard Picart, in Amsterdam.

Giovanni Boldini's father painted religious subjects, and his older brother Luigi became an architect. In 1862 he went to Florence for six years, rarely attended the Academy of Fine Arts, but met the Macchiaioli painters there. Their influence shows in his landscapes, though he became best known for his portraits. In London he painted members of society, including Lady Holland and the Duchess of Westminster. From 1872 he lived in Paris, where he became a friend of Edgar Degas. Time magazine said he was known as the Master of Swish because of his flowing style.

Johann Friedrich Bause was self-taught at first. In 1759 he worked briefly in Augsburg under Johann Jacob Haid, and there he met the portrait painter Anton Graff. His inspiration came from the German engraver Johann Georg Wille, who lived abroad. He moved from Halle to Leipzig in 1766, where he became a professor of copper engraving and specialized in portraits. He made his last engraving in 1809, when his eyesight was beginning to fail. Later he followed his daughter Juliane, an engraver and painter herself, to Weimar, where he died.

Quirijn van Brekelenkam probably studied under Gerard Dou, so his paintings are similar to those of the Leiden fijnschilders. Not much is certain about his life. He was probably born in Zwammerdam, because his sister Aeltgen was born there. He registered with the Guild of Saint Luke in Leiden in 1648, the same year as his earliest known painting. He married twice and had six children with his first wife and three with his second. His last known painting, De goudweger, dates from 1668.

Arnold van Westerhout's father placed him as a boy with the Antwerp artist Alexander Goetiers, because he showed a talent for drawing. In Antwerp he worked mainly as a draughtsman and as an engraver of portraits. By 1679 he was living in Venice, where he worked for a publisher. He later settled in Rome, in the home of the Dutch engraver Cornelis Bloemaert, who named him executor of his will. In 1687 he bought the stock of the French print publisher François Collignon. One big job was the illustrations for Giovanni Ciampini's Vetera Monimenta, published in 1690.

Auguste Hüssener came from Szczecin and learned under the engraver Ludwig Buchhorn. In 1814 she became a professor at the Prussian Academy of Arts, and from 1824 she led its School of Engraving. She showed work at the Academy's annual exhibitions for decades. Her portraits showed people from the aristocracy, art, diplomacy and science. She gave special attention to women of her day, such as Jenny Lind and Lola Montez. Her sisters also worked in Berlin.

Willem van de Velde the Elder drew precise pictures of ships and made ink paintings of fleets, but later he learned to use oil paints like his son. He came from Leiden, the son of a Flemish skipper, and he is commonly said to have been raised for the sea. He married Judith Adriaens van Leeuwen in 1631. Two of their sons became painters, Willem the Younger at sea and Adriaen on land. His marriage was stormy, and a legal separation followed his affair with a married woman.

Cornelis Pietersz Bega spent his whole life in Haarlem. His father was a sculptor and goldsmith, and his mother was the illegitimate daughter of the painter Cornelis van Haarlem. He studied under Adriaen van Ostade and painted similar genre scenes, usually groups of a few peasants in interiors, or fanciful figures such as The Alchemist. From 1653 to 1654 he went on a Grand Tour with fellow painters through Germany, Switzerland and France. He joined the Haarlem Guild of Saint Luke in 1654. He died ten years later, and Houbraken blamed the plague.

Benoît-Louis Prévost trained with the engraver Jean Ouvrier, and he was a more skilled craftsman than his master. He engraved more than sixty of Charles Nicolas Cochin's drawings with great care and precision. His best-known work is the frontispiece of the Encyclopédie edited by Diderot and d'Alembert, made after a drawing by Cochin. It shows Reason and Philosophy. He also made portraits of Louis XV, Marie Antoinette and Louis XVI, all from works by Cochin. From works by Jean-Michel Moreau he engraved a portrait of Joseph Ignace Guillotin.

Adolf Schreyer studied art at the Städel Institute in his native Frankfurt and then at Stuttgart and Munich. He first travelled with Maximilian Karl, Prince of Thurn and Taxis, through Hungary, Wallachia and Turkey. In 1854 he followed the Austrian army across the Wallachian frontier. He also went to Egypt and Syria. He settled in Paris but went back to Germany in 1870, and he died at Kronberg im Taunus near Frankfurt. He painted horses, peasant life in Wallachia and Moldavia, and battle scenes, and the Vanderbilt and Astor families were among his collectors.

François Marius Granet's father was a small builder in Aix-en-Provence. An Italian artist passing through gave him some first lessons, and his parents then put him in a free art school run by the landscape painter Jean-Antoine Constantin. In 1797 he went to Paris at the invitation of the comte de Forbin and entered the studio of Jacques-Louis David. He got a cell in the Capuchin convent, which almost only artists lived in. In 1821 he gave Alexander I of Russia his view of the choir of the Capuchin church in Rome. He kept returning to Rome.

Giovanni Battista Piazzetta got his first training in wood carving from his father, the sculptor Giacomo Piazzetta. Starting in 1697 he studied with the painter Antonio Molinari. By his own account he also studied under Giuseppe Maria Crespi in Bologna, though Crespi left no record of teaching him. Around 1710 he returned to Venice. Collectors bought his drawings of half-length figures and groups of heads as works in their own right. One of his best-known paintings is The Soothsayer, in the Gallerie dell'Accademia in Venice.

Joachim Wtewael made good money as a flax merchant and sat on the Utrecht town council, and he painted too. He trained in the style of late 16th-century Haarlem Mannerism and stayed faithful to it. He left about a hundred paintings, large ones on canvas and tiny ones on copper plates, which are the more numerous. His subjects were religious and mythological, and the mythological ones have a strong erotic element. Emperor Rudolf II obtained his Golden Age. His best-known work is the near life-size Perseus and Andromeda in the Louvre.

John Greenwood's father died insolvent in 1742, and about then the boy was apprenticed to Thomas Johnston, a Boston line engraver and sign painter. He soon left to pursue portraits. He sailed to Surinam, stayed there more than five years, and painted 115 portraits. After that he settled in Amsterdam for a time to learn to make mezzotints. He then stayed in Paris and finally settled in London in 1764. Later he made trips to buy paintings, including one for the Earl of Bute.

Both of Fritz Bamberger's parents were Bavarian musicians, and he was their fourth son. He moved to Frankfurt with them in 1820, and his sister Sabine became an opera singer there. He studied painting under Johann Georg Primavesi in Kassel, at the Prussian Academy of Arts, and in Munich under Carl Rottmann. A trip to France and England in 1836 gave him material for The Battlefield of Hastings. After three years in the artillery corps in Würzburg he returned to Frankfurt and began painting again. Several trips to Spain changed his career, and he specialized in Spanish landscapes.

Alfred Philippe Roll studied at the École des Beaux-Arts under Jean-Léon Gérôme and Léon Bonnat, among others. He served as a lieutenant of militia. His painting The Flood at Toulouse drew huge attention in 1875. After he showed Fête of Silenus in 1877, he decided to paint everyday life, in a more realist style. His 1880 painting Miner's Strike made him one of the highest ranked painters in France. He became an official painter of the French government and was commissioned for murals, ceilings and other building decoration.

Edwin Lord Weeks's parents were spice and tea merchants from Newton, and they paid for his youthful interest in painting and travel. In 1872 he moved to Paris and became a pupil of Léon Bonnat and Jean-Léon Gérôme. He emerged as one of America's major painters of Orientalist subjects. He was an inveterate traveler. His journeys took him to Egypt, Persia, Morocco and India. In India he was the first known American artist to visit, and he sketched and painted daily life and royalty.

Harriet Backer grew up as one of four daughters in a well-off family at Holmestrand. Her father was a shipping merchant, and the family moved to Christiania, now Oslo, in 1856. At twelve she had her first lessons. Later she studied with Johan Fredrik Eckersberg and in Berlin, and then in Munich with Eilif Peterssen at the Academy of Fine Arts, before she went on to Paris and became a student of Léon Bonnat and Jean-Léon Gérôme. She is best known for her detailed interior scenes.

Sanford Gifford grew up in Hudson, New York, as the fourth of eleven children of a Quaker ironmaker. He left Brown University. In 1845 he moved to New York City to study art, learning drawing, perspective and anatomy under John Rubens Smith and taking drawing classes at the National Academy of Design. He was trained as a portrait painter, but the first work he showed at the Academy was a landscape. After that he devoted himself mainly to landscape painting. The Academy elected him an Associate in 1851 and a full Academician in 1854.

The painter Andrea Camassei saw the drawings of young Carlo Maratta and encouraged him to go to Rome. He moved there in 1636 with a family friend, and his half-brother Bernabeo, an unsuccessful painter, hosted him. Bernabeo introduced him to Andrea Sacchi, and Maratta stayed in Sacchi's workshop until his master died in 1661. He copied the Antique. His fresco Constantine Ordering the Destruction of Pagan Idols, based on designs by Sacchi, gained him attention. His first independent public work in Rome was an Adoration of the Shepherds.

Paul Gabriël belonged to the Hague School. His father, a sculptor, died when Paul was five. At twelve he enrolled in the sculpture class at the Royal Academy in Amsterdam, but he left without taking an exam. In 1844 his guardians sent him to the drawing college of B.C. Koekkoek in Kleve, where he stayed for about a year and was not keen on the training. He then took lessons from the landscape painter Cornelis Lieste in Haarlem, where Anton Mauve became a good friend. He earned his money with pencil portraits that he sold for ten to twelve guilders.

Johann Georg Mentzel learned his craft from Erasmus Andresohn. He made many copper engravings, mostly portraits. His sitters ranged from Empress Anna Ivanovna, Frederick William I of Prussia and Augustus II of Poland to scholars such as Cesare Cremonini and Johann Heinrich Feustking. He also illustrated books, among them Carl Christian Schramm's Saxonia monumentis viarum illustrata of 1726 and Johann Georg Wachter's Archaeologia Nummaria of 1740. Many of his portraits are in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.

Johann Martin Will started out as a miller's journeyman. He settled in Augsburg, where he married and in 1755 founded a publishing house for copper engravings. It put out costume pictures and children's games, cut-out sheets, devotional images, portrait engravings, caricatures and historical scenes, plus a few maps. His eldest daughter married the miniature painter Johann Walch, who joined the firm, and the firm turned more to maps. In 1789 it bought the stock of the map publishers Matthäus Seutter and Tobias Conrad Lotter, almost 25,000 sheets and 208 copper plates. Walch inherited the business after Will died.

Johann Georg Pforr first meant to follow his father, a tenant farmer. War made the family poor, so he worked in the Richelsdorf mines. In 1769 he met the director of the porcelain factory in Kassel, who hired him as a porcelain painter, and two years later he left to run his parents' estate. In 1778 he visited the new art academy in Kassel. A year later he became a member. His contemporaries called him the German Wouwerman, because he specialized in painting horses.

Giovanni Francesco Costa started in Venice as a painter of perspective views. He studied with the stage designers Gerolamo Mengozzi-Colonna and Giambattista Crosato and then made his name as a stage designer, above all for the Grimani theatres in Venice. In 1743 he published ten etchings of ancient arches, temples, baths and tombs. Between 1750 and 1756 he brought out Delle delicie del fiume Brenta, a set of 140 engravings of the grand houses of Venetian nobles along the river. He measured the buildings with the help of a camera obscura.

Theodor Jachimowicz grew up as the son of a Greek Catholic priest and studied painting at the Vienna Academy. He worked as a theater painter, from 1827 at the Leopoldstadt Theater, then at the Theater in der Josefstadt, and from 1851 to 1870 at the court opera in the Kärntnertor theater. He exhibited at the Vienna Academy. He painted mostly oils and watercolours of religious subjects, altarpieces and interiors of Viennese churches. He also made an iconostasis with 75 saints' pictures for a Greek Catholic monastery church in Zahlé in Lebanon.

Carl Theodor Reiffenstein's father was a brewer who wanted him to take over the family tavern, but the boy liked art, so he got a live-in drawing tutor. In 1828 he and his teacher took a trip around Hofheim, Lorsbach and Eppstein. By 1830 he was already hand coloring lithographs for pay. At thirteen he enrolled at the Städelschule, first planning to become an architect, and then he switched to painting. Later he wandered through the old town of Frankfurt, and he sketched buildings sometimes only days before they were razed. His known works number over 2,000, mostly watercolors.

Louis-Gabriel Moreau is called Moreau the elder, to tell him apart from his younger brother Jean-Michel Moreau. He was a pupil of Pierre-Antoine Demachy, and like Demachy he focused on buildings and the countryside in and around Paris. He mostly painted in gouache. His work was first shown in 1760 at the Exposition de la Jeunesse. The Royal Academy turned him down in 1787 and again in 1788, possibly because it did not share his preference for landscapes. He worked for the Count of Artois, and for several years he lived in the Louvre.

Giovanni Antonio Pellegrini's father was a shoemaker from Padua. Pellegrini was a pupil of the Milanese painter Paolo Pagani and went with him to Moravia and Vienna. He was back in Venice in 1696, and there he painted his first surviving works. He married Angela Carriera, the sister of Rosalba Carriera. The Earl of Manchester invited him to England, where he stayed from 1708 to 1713, and he later traveled on commissions to the Southern Netherlands, the Dutch Republic, Germany, Austria and France. One of his pupils was Antonio Visentini.

Petrus van Geldorp's father, Wilhelmus Petrus, was a painter of mostly religious art. At thirteen the boy went to a Franciscan boarding school in Megen, but he left after three years because he did not want to become a priest. He studied at the Rijksakademie in Amsterdam and had private lessons from his father. He drew political cartoons for the newspapers De Tijd and De Amsterdamsche Courant, and his anti-socialist views sometimes showed through. He also illustrated magazines and children's books and designed advertising. For the publisher Malmberg he made school wall charts.

After his training and travels in Italy, Pieter Bruegel the Elder returned in 1555 to settle in Antwerp. There he worked mainly as a designer of prints for a publisher. Later he made painting his main medium. He is known for landscapes and peasant scenes, and he was a pioneer in presenting both kinds of subject as large paintings. He also painted no portraits. Landscape with the Fall of Icarus and The Hunters in the Snow have inspired writers and filmmakers.

Timothy Cole came to the United States from London as a boy. He lost everything he owned in the Chicago fire of 1871. In 1875 he moved to New York and found work at the Century magazine, which was then called Scribner's, and he stayed with it for 40 years. In 1883 his publishers sent him abroad to engrave a set of blocks after the old masters in the European galleries. He published his prints in books such as Old Italian Masters and Old Dutch and Flemish Masters. He was a pioneer craftsman of wood engraving.

Johann Peter Krafft's father was an enamel painter, and his brother Joseph also became a painter of portrait miniatures. By ten he was already attending drawing school. In 1799 he was sent to an aunt in Vienna, where he enrolled at the Academy of Fine Arts and studied history painting with Heinrich Friedrich Füger. A trip to Paris in 1802 introduced him to Jacques-Louis David and François Gérard, who strongly influenced his style. Back in Vienna in 1805, he settled as a portrait painter. He married Juliana Preisinger, and three of their children became painters.

Pierre-François Basan got his first drawing lessons from the engraver Étienne Fessard, a cousin of his mother. Later he studied with Jean Daullé. For several years he worked on large projects, such as the illustrations for Buffon's Histoire Naturelle. After 1754 he gave himself almost entirely to publishing and selling prints, and he built a commercial network across Europe that lasted until 1788. He focused on the younger generation of engravers. In 1786 he bought seventy-six original plates by Rembrandt from the estate of the collector Claude-Henri Watelet.

Nicaise de Keyser studied painting at the Antwerp Academy of Fine Arts under Jacob Jacobs and Mattheus Ignatius van Bree. After 1835 he traveled a lot, including to England, Scotland, Paris and Italy. He married the genre painter Isabella Telghuys. In 1855 the Romantic painter Gustave Wappers resigned as director of the Antwerp Academy, and de Keyser took his place. Viewers in German-speaking Europe liked his history paintings in particular, and in 1873 he received the Prussian order Pour le Mérite. He had many students, among them Léon Abry and Aloïs Boudry.

Pontarlier, where François Perrier was born, belonged then to the County of Burgundy and not to France. From 1620 to 1625 he lived in Rome, where he took Giovanni Lanfranco as his model while Lanfranco worked on the dome of Sant'Andrea della Valle. After a brief stay in Lyon he settled in Paris in 1630, where he worked in the circle of Simon Vouet. Charles Le Brun was briefly his pupil. His two collections of prints after antique sculptures gave generations of artists classical models to copy.

Jean-Michel Moreau, called Moreau le Jeune, went to St Petersburg in 1758 with his teacher Louis-Joseph Le Lorrain. He taught drawing there briefly. He came back to Paris in 1759 after the sudden death of Le Lorrain and then worked for the engraver Jacques-Philippe Lebas, making drawings of paintings for engravers to work from. For the Encyclopédie of Diderot and d'Alembert he made pen and wash drawings of artisanal processes. He collaborated with François Boucher and Hubert Gravelot on illustrations for an edition of Ovid's Metamorphoses.

Bartholomeus van der Helst grew up in Haarlem. His father was an innkeeper, and he had moved to Amsterdam some time before 1636, the year he married the 18-year-old orphan Anna du Pire, who came from a prosperous family of the Southern Netherlands. The couple had six children, and their son Lodewijk also became a portrait painter. His first dated picture, the Regents of the Walloon Orphanage in Amsterdam, is from 1637. In Amsterdam he may have trained with Nicolaes Eliaszoon Pickenoy. His portraits won him the patronage of Amsterdam's elite and the Stadtholder's circle.

Martin Monnickendam's early work is mostly animal drawings made at Natura Artis Magistra. He trained at the Rijksakademie in Amsterdam from 1891 and then studied in Paris, and he won various awards and took study trips to London and Italy. Today his work is seen as being in the school of George Breitner. The Stedelijk Museum held an honorary show for his 50th birthday. He died in Amsterdam in 1943. He was poor and waiting to be deported as a Jew.

Jean-Antoine Linck learned his craft first from his father, Jean-Conrad Linck, an enamel painter and engraver in Geneva. The engraver Carl Hackert later trained him, together with Wolfgang Adam Toepffer. He opened his own studio in 1802. His works show the area around Geneva and the Alps, and they follow those of Johann Ludwig Aberli. They were a clear success with Joséphine de Beauharnais and Catherine II, at a time when Alpine tourism was growing. His brother Jean-Philippe, a painter and engraver, mostly reproduced his works.
